claims.text: Pt, Ir, or Ru precursor salts reduce early during synthesis.
Early-reduced Pt, Ir, or Ru rapidly forms an initial lattice.
The initial noble-metal lattice promotes adsorption and dissociation of H2.
Reactive hydrogen generated on the initial lattice reduces adjacent Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe ions.
The reduced transition metals incorporate into the pre-existing noble-metal lattice to produce a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Pd-containing systems fail to form uniform alloys because Pd provides less favorable hydrogen desorption and higher reduction barriers.
Systems lacking a noble metal fail to form uniform alloys because they lack hydrogen-assisted reduction and lattice seeding.
Spray drying the homogeneously mixed salts produces near-spherical precursor particles.
The spray-dried precursor particles are compositionally uniform.
The SD-TDR treatment forms porous, self-supported three-dimensional nanoframeworks assembled from nanoarms.
The resulting nanoframeworks have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The resulting lattice can contain fcc, hcp, or mixed fcc/hcp structures depending on Pt or Ru content and post-synthesis heating.
Increasing Ru content systematically increases the fraction of the Ru-hcp phase.
Secondary heating systematically drives an fcc-to-hcp conversion.
HEA nanoparticles synthesized by the proposed method will have greater methanol oxidation mass activity than commercial Pt black and Pt-rich or untreated alloys.
The synthesized HEA nanoparticles will sustain a higher methanol-oxidation current than the baselines.
The predicted catalytic improvement arises from a larger electrochemically active surface area and homogeneous elemental distribution.
Commercial Pt black has a methanol oxidation mass activity of 170 mA/mgPt.
Commercial Pt black has an electrochemically active surface area of 17.59 m2/gPt.
The proposed mechanism applies to Pt-, Ir-, or Ru-seeded mixtures containing up to eight elements and Pt:Ru ratios from 3:1 to 1:4.
